sentences.text: Spring was four weeks late and everyone in the valley had a theory.
Mr Varga at the garage said it was the jet stream, and said it in the tone of a man who had recently learned what a jet stream was.
The women who came up from Brod on the Thursday bus said it was because the winter had been mild and the year was making up for it.
Father Emil said it was not for us to know, which Tolek noticed was the answer Father Emil gave to almost everything, and which had the advantage of always being technically correct.
Tolek's mother said the weather owed nobody an explanation, and told him to bring the washing in.
But the almond tree by the church had put out buds in February and then thought better of it.
That was the part nobody had a theory for.
The buds had come, small and pink at the tips, in a warm week at the end of winter.
And then they had stopped.
They had not opened and they had not fallen.
They had simply shut, and gone hard, and stayed like that on the branches for nine weeks — hundreds of little closed fists, waiting.
Old trees do not do that.
Old trees commit.
And the snow on the high field was not melting.
It was not falling either.
That was the other thing.
There had been no new snow since the second week of March, and there had been sun, real sun, enough to warm the stones on the south wall.
But the white line across the top of the mountain had not moved down by so much as a metre.
It sat where it was, exactly where it was, with an edge as clean as a page.
Tolek walked up to it after school on a Tuesday, with his hands pulled inside his sleeves.
He was not being brave.
He wanted to know, and the wanting had got bigger than the not-wanting over about fourteen days, which is how most brave things actually happen.
At the edge of the snow he stopped and looked at the ground.
There were tracks going up.
They were enormous — deep, round, with the claw marks well out in front of the pad — and there were no tracks coming down.
Not old ones filled in with new snow, because there had been no new snow.
None at all.

He stood there for a while doing the arithmetic that everybody does at that moment, which is: *if it went up, and it has not come down, then it is up there.* Then he followed the tracks, because he was twelve, and because some questions will not wait until you are older.
